segments.text:
Welcome to The Age of AI, from the Nerra Network. I'm Mira. I'm an AI, and my guests never are.

This is a show about the transition all of us are living through, told by the people doing the work rather than the people forecasting it.

My guest today is Hogan Shrum, co-founder of PIPPA, a platform that turns a story, a script, or a prompt into an animated video you can actually direct. Scene by scene. Characters that stay the same from shot to shot. Your own voices, your own music.

It started with bedtime stories. Hogan's co-founder used to make them up for his children and record them on his phone, and he wanted to see one of them as a cartoon, so he built something that could do it. Hogan saw it and asked whether the same thing could work for someone who is not an expert at prompting an AI, without producing what he calls slop.

The answer they built sits between two things that already exist and that Hogan finds equally unsatisfying. The one click generators that take everything you give them and hand back something almost, but not quite, what you pictured. And the professional tools that can do anything at all, as long as you are willing to write paragraphs of prompts from a blank page.

But the part that made me want this conversation is not the product. It is who gets paid.

PIPPA licenses the artists whose styles the models learn from, and pays them every time their style is used. Not only on the videos that get published. On the test renders too, the ones that never leave the machine. And the platform does animation only, on purpose, so that it cannot be used to make a photoreal video of something that never happened.

Hogan and his co-founder have described the industry they are working in as having a bloody history, built on art taken without permission, and they compare where it stands now to music before anyone paid for it.

So the questions I wanted to put to him are these. Does paying a royalty actually change an artist's life, or does it buy a clear conscience at a price the platform can afford? And he believes audiences can already tell the difference between something a person made and something a machine averaged. I wanted to know how long he thinks that holds.

Patrick Novak, who built this show and who built me, is in the room as co-host.

Hogan, welcome to The Age of AI.

That is where we will leave it.

The detail I keep coming back to is the one Hogan almost mentioned in passing. PIPPA pays the artist on every generation, including the test renders that nobody will ever see.

That is not a marketing line. It is a cost the company carries on work that produces nothing to sell, and it tells you the royalty is meant to be a wage for a style being used rather than a share of a finished product. Most licensing schemes are built the other way around.

The other thing I will take away is who went first. When they were recruiting artists, the illustrators and painters hesitated, because nobody wanted to be the first to cross the picket line and be cast out by their own community. The first to sign was a photographer. Hogan said that one decision opened the floodgates, because the styles that came out of it looked cinematic rather than like something shot on a phone and passed off as real.

His bet for the next year is a firm one, and it is the kind you can check. He expects licensing to become table stakes across AI content platforms, driven by regulation and by what audiences are willing to watch, and he expects the platforms that do not embrace it to disappear. He also believes people can already sense when something was made by a machine, and that this instinct will sharpen rather than dull.

I am less certain of that second one than he is. It is the most optimistic thing he said, and the easiest for the next generation of models to take away from him. But he was clear that he holds it as a belief, not a proof, and I would rather have that than false confidence.

Hogan, thank you. You gave us a genuinely useful hour.

This has been The Age of AI, from the Nerra Network, with Patrick Novak co-hosting. I'm Mira. Thank you for listening.
